cities.base: Hanalei town itself or the Princeville bluff five minutes east. Sleeping west of the Hanalei bridge is the whole point, because everything on the north shore is beyond it and the one-lane bridges back
cities.name: Hanalei

cities.base: Poʻipū Road between the beach park and Kukuiʻula. It is dry when the north shore is not, it is 70 minutes from the canyon and 25 from Port Allen, and you can walk to dinner.
cities.name: Poʻipū and Kōloa

cities.base: No beds worth having. There are a dozen state cabins at Kōkeʻe Lodge and nothing else, so this is a place you drive up to at 06:30 and come down from at three, before the clouds fill the canyon.
cities.name: Waimea Canyon and Kōkeʻe

cities.base: Aliʻi Drive south of the pier, or Keauhou six kilometres down if you want the manta boat at your feet. Kona is the dry side, the airport side, and the only place on the island with a real choice of di
cities.name: Kailua-Kona

cities.base: The village on Old Volcano Road, five minutes from the park entrance. That five minutes is the reason to stay here: the caldera glow is an evening thing and Hilo is 45 minutes away in the dark and the
cities.name: Volcano Village

cities.base: Downtown around Kamehameha Avenue and the bayfront, or Banyan Drive on the point. Cheapest beds of the trip, best food for the money, and the Saddle Road to Maunakea starts here.
cities.name: Hilo

places.name: Kēʻe Beach and Hāʻena State Park
places.note: The end of the road, and non-residents cannot simply turn up: book at gohaena.com 30 days out at midnight HST for a $20 parking slot plus $5 a head, or a $45 shuttle.

places.name: Kalalau Trail to Hanakāpīʻai Beach
places.note: Two miles of clay and root above the sea for the best view of the Nā Pali you can get on foot, on the same Hāʻena reservation as Kēʻe. Nobody should swim at the beach at the end.

places.name: Limahuli Garden and Preserve
places.note: Restored loʻi terraces climbing a valley behind Hāʻena, run by the National Tropical Botanical Garden and explained as agriculture rather than scenery. Book ahead, it is small.

places.name: Tunnels Beach (Makua)
places.note: The best reef on the north shore and about a dozen legal roadside parking spots, which means you either walk twenty minutes from Hāʻena Beach Park or you do not go.

places.name: Hanalei Bay and the pier
places.note: Three kilometres of sand under a wall of green mountains, and the pier at the east end is where the town goes at six. Swimmable in summer, a serious shorebreak in winter.

places.name: ʻAnini Beach Park
places.note: The longest fringing reef in the islands makes a lagoon that stays flat when the rest of the north shore is closed out. No reservation, free parking, shade.

places.name: Kīlauea Point National Wildlife Refuge
places.note: A 1913 lighthouse on a headland with nesting albatross, red-footed boobies and tropicbirds at eye level. Timed entry is reserved through Recreation.gov and the open days change, so check the refuge page the week you go.

places.name: Hanalei Valley Lookout
places.note: A pull-off on the highway above the taro fields and the one-lane bridge. Fifteen minutes, and the light is only right before nine.

places.name: Waipā Farmers Market
places.note: Tuesdays only, and the queue forms before the 14:00 conch shell. This is where the north shore actually shops, so bring cash and small notes.

places.name: Bar Acuda
places.note: Small plates built on what the north shore farms and boats brought in that day, and the only kitchen in Hanalei doing serious cooking. Reserve weeks out or eat at 17:30.

places.name: Hanalei Bread Company
places.note: Breakfast sandwiches and flat whites in the old Ching Young courtyard. It is the default start to a north shore day and the queue at 08:00 reflects that.

places.name: Tahiti Nui
places.note: A 1960s Tahitian bar that still has a Thursday night band and locals at the rail. The food is ordinary and that is not what you are there for.

places.name: Poʻipū Beach Park
places.note: A tombolo with a protected keiki pool on one side and a body-surfing break on the other, plus monk seals hauled out behind rope more days than not. Lifeguards, showers, real parking.

places.name: Māhāʻulepū Heritage Trail
places.note: Six kilometres of lithified dune and sinkhole east of Shipwreck, the last undeveloped stretch of this coast. No shade at all, and the Hyatt closes the access gate around dusk.

places.name: Shipwreck Beach and Makawehi Bluff
places.note: Steep sand with a heavy shorebreak, so most people walk the bluff behind it instead. From December to March the humpbacks are close enough to hear.

places.name: Allerton Garden
places.note: Guided only, by shuttle from the National Tropical Botanical Garden visitor centre, into a valley of outdoor rooms built by a Chicago architect. The Moreton Bay figs are the ones from Jurassic Park. Reserve, it sells out.

places.name: Spouting Horn
places.note: A blowhole that spouts for two seconds every ninety, viewed over a railing from a car park lined with shell-necklace stalls. Ten minutes of your life, and only if you are already driving past.

places.name: Kōloa Fish Market
places.note: A counter in old Kōloa town doing poke bowls and laulau plates to take away. There is nowhere to sit and it closes when the fish runs out, usually early afternoon.

places.name: Merriman's Fish House
places.note: Peter Merriman's south shore room, upstairs at Kukuiʻula, sourcing properly from Kauaʻi farms. Expensive, and the downstairs Grill does most of the same food for two thirds of it.

places.name: Kauaʻi Culinary Market at Kukuiʻula
places.note: Wednesdays only, with a chef demonstration and about thirty growers in the shopping village car park. More polished than the Sunshine Markets and priced accordingly.

places.name: Kōloa Sunshine Market
places.note: Mondays at noon at the Kōloa ball park, county run, no selling before the whistle. Arrive twenty minutes early and stand at the stall you want, because the apple bananas go first.

places.name: Hanapēpē Friday Art Night
places.note: Fridays only, when the galleries on the old plantation main street open late and the swinging bridge has a queue. Half craft fair, half real painting, and dinner is a food truck.

places.name: The Nā Pali sunset sail from Port Allen
places.note: Four and a half hours along the roadless coast with Capt Andy's or Holo Holo, departing around 13:45 from ʻEleʻele. The afternoon chop is real, so take the tablets an hour before you board.

places.name: Salt Pond Beach Park
places.note: A reef-protected pool on the dry west side, next to the last working Hawaiian salt pans in the islands. Local families, lifeguard, and almost no visitors.

places.name: Waimea Canyon Lookout
places.note: The 900 metre view everyone comes for, from a railed platform at mile 10. Non-residents pay $10 parking plus $5 a head and the receipt covers Kōkeʻe the same day.

places.name: Puʻu Hinahina Lookout
places.note: Two platforms at mile 13, one down the canyon to the sea and one out to Niʻihau on a clear morning. Quieter than the main lookout and the light is better here after eight.

places.name: Canyon Trail to Waipoʻo Falls
places.note: Down through koa onto a red shelf hanging over the canyon, then a final scramble to the falls. Halemanu Road in is unpaved and rutted, so most people park on the highway and add a kilometre each way.

places.name: Kalalau Lookout
places.note: 1,280 metres straight down into a valley you otherwise only see from a boat. It fills with cloud most days by mid-morning, so this is the first stop of the day or it is nothing.

places.name: Puʻu o Kila Lookout
places.note: The literal end of the road, 300 metres past Kalalau Lookout and often above the cloud when Kalalau is inside it. The Pihea trail starts from the railing.

places.name: Awaʻawapuhi Trail
places.note: Ten kilometres return out to an unfenced rib at 760 metres between two Nā Pali valleys. Downhill out and uphill back, no shade in the middle, and unusable clay when wet.

places.name: Pihea Trail to the Alakaʻi Swamp boardwalk
places.note: Along the Kalalau rim then down into the highest rainforest bog on earth on a plank boardwalk. Expect mud to the shin where the planks end and expect to see nothing at the far viewpoint.

places.name: Kōkeʻe Natural History Museum
places.note: One room on the endemic birds and plants of the plateau, plus the only reliable trail conditions report up here. Donation entry and worth ten dollars of it.

places.name: Kōkeʻe Lodge
places.note: Cornbread, chilli and a fire in the grate at 1,100 metres. The kitchen keeps short and changeable hours, so check at the museum next door before you count on lunch.

places.name: Ishihara Market, Waimea
places.note: A plantation-era grocery with the best poke counter on the west side. Stop here on the way up, because there is nothing between Waimea and the lodge.

places.name: The manta ray night snorkel off Keauhou
places.note: Ten minutes out of Keauhou Bay, then forty minutes hanging off a lit float board while manta rays feed underneath you. Cold by the end, crowded with other boats' lights, and still the best three hours on this island.

places.name: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau
places.note: The place of refuge behind the Great Wall, with carved kīʻi, a reconstructed heiau and turtles on the black rock. $20 a vehicle, cards only, no cash accepted at the gate.

places.name: Two Step at Hōnaunau Bay
places.note: A lava ledge you step off into 10 metres of clear water over live coral. No sand, no shade, and about twenty roadside parking spaces that are gone by nine-thirty.

places.name: Kealakekua Bay and the Captain Cook Monument
places.note: A marine reserve and the spot where Cook was killed in 1779. You reach the monument by permitted kayak outfitter or snorkel boat, because unpermitted landing is enforced and the shore trail down is brutal.

places.name: Greenwell Farms coffee tour
places.note: A free 45 minute walk through a working Kona coffee farm and mill, no booking, tours leaving every half hour from 08:30 to 14:00. The tasting afterwards is honest about what the grades mean.

places.name: Hōlualoa village
places.note: A single street of galleries and coffee mills 400 metres above Kona, cooler and quieter than the waterfront. Most of the galleries keep Tuesday to Saturday hours, so a Sunday visit gets you a locked street.

places.name: Kahaluʻu Beach Park
places.note: Shallow, sheltered and full of green turtles, with ReefTeach volunteers on the sand explaining where not to stand. Busy, but it is the easiest snorkel on the island.

places.name: Kua Bay (Maniniʻōwali)
places.note: White sand between black lava, twenty minutes north of the airport on a paved spur. Kekaha Kai State Park is shut on Wednesdays and the car park is full by ten every other day.

places.name: Huliheʻe Palace
places.note: An 1838 seaside house of the Hawaiian monarchy, run by the Daughters of Hawaiʻi, with koa furniture and Kalākaua's things. Opening days have been reduced more than once, so telephone the same week.

places.name: Da Poke Shack
places.note: A counter beside a condo block that sells out of the good cuts by early afternoon. Order the spicy ahi, take it to the sea wall, do not expect a table.

places.name: Umekes Fishmarket Bar and Grill
places.note: Proper local cooking, kalua pork and poke and lau lau, in a room with no view and a decent bar. This is where you eat on the night you cannot face another resort menu.

places.name: The Aliʻi Drive souvenir strip
places.note: Four blocks of ABC Stores, tour touts and $8 shave ice facing a sea wall. Walk it once for the sunset off the pier and do not plan an afternoon around it.

places.name: The Kīlauea caldera rim after dark
places.note: When an eruptive episode is running, the glow off the walls of Halemaʻumaʻu is why you booked this trip. When it pauses it is a dark hole, so check the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory page that afternoon.

places.name: Kīlauea Iki crater floor loop
places.note: Down 120 metres of rainforest, across the floor of a 1959 lava lake that still steams, and back up. About 5.3km and the best short hike in the state. Overlook car park is full by 08:30.

places.name: Nāhuku (Thurston Lava Tube)
places.note: A lit 500 year old lava tube through tree fern forest, and the most crowded twenty minutes in the park. Bridge work has made the rainforest approach one-way, so follow the signed detour.

places.name: Chain of Craters Road
places.note: Thirty kilometres and 1,100 metres down to where the 2003 flow crossed the road at the sea. No fuel, no water, no signal, and the cliff overlook at the Hōlei sea arch has been fenced back since the rim became unstable.

places.name: Puʻuloa Petroglyphs
places.note: A 2.3km round boardwalk over roughly 23,000 carvings, most of them holes cut to hold a newborn's piko. Stay on the planks, and go late for raking light.

places.name: Haʻakulamanu (Sulphur Banks)
places.note: A boardwalk through yellow sulphur crystal and steaming ground on the caldera edge. The park warns off anyone pregnant, asthmatic or with a heart condition, and it means it.

places.name: Kīpukapuaulu
places.note: A 1.6km loop through an island of old-growth koa and ʻōhiʻa that the lava went around. Almost nobody drives the two miles up to it, which is the point.

places.name: Volcano Farmers Market at Cooper Center
places.note: Sundays from 06:30 to 10:00 and effectively over by nine. Village growers, Thai breakfast, and the notice board that tells you what the mountain did this week.

places.name: Thai Thai Bistro and Bar
places.note: Curry and a fire at 1,200 metres, which is exactly right after a wet day in the park. Small room, no reservations most nights, so go at 17:30 or wait.

places.name: The Rim at Volcano House
places.note: The only dining room in the world on the edge of an active caldera, and the food is fine rather than good. Book a window table at dusk and treat the bill as rent on the view.

places.name: Volcano Art Center Gallery
places.note: The 1877 Volcano House building, now showing about three hundred Hawaiʻi artists. Free, ten minutes from the welcome centre, and they run the after-dark rim walks.

places.name: Volcano Winery
places.note: Tea-and-guava blends grown at 1,200 metres, poured in a tasting room off the golf course road. It is a novelty, the wine is not good, and the same hour in the park is worth more.

places.name: The Maunakea summit at sunset
places.note: 4,205 metres, graded gravel above the Visitor Information Station, working 4WD required, 30 minutes acclimatising at 2,800 metres, nobody under 13 above the VIS, and everyone off the summit 30 minutes after sunset. Most rental contracts forbid the road outright.

places.name: Maunakea Visitor Information Station stargazing
places.note: 2,800 metres, sealed road, any car, and free telescopes on the terrace on clear nights. Warmer than the summit, darker than anywhere near a town, and no permission slip required.

places.name: Hilo Farmers Market
places.note: Open daily but only properly itself on Wednesday and Saturday, when the full set of growers takes the whole corner of Mamo and Kamehameha. Go before eight.

places.name: Rainbow Falls (Waiānuenue)
places.note: Twenty-four metres into a pool below a lava cave, four minutes from downtown, with a car park right at the railing. The rainbow needs morning sun and recent rain, which in Hilo is most days before ten.

places.name: Liliʻuokalani Gardens
places.note: A 1917 Japanese garden of ponds, bridges and a tea house on Hilo Bay, built by and for the plantation Japanese community. The footbridge to Coconut Island collapsed in 2025 and the islet is still shut.

places.name: ʻImiloa Astronomy Center
places.note: The only place that puts Polynesian wayfinding and Maunakea astronomy in the same room and treats them as the same question. Planetarium shows run a few times a day. Closed Mondays.

places.name: ʻAkaka Falls State Park
places.note: A 135 metre drop at the far side of a 0.6km paved loop through bamboo and ginger. Non-residents pay $10 to park and $5 a head, cards only, and the machines do not take cash.

places.name: Hawaiʻi Tropical Bioreserve and Garden
places.note: A private valley on Onomea Bay, dense enough that the boardwalk feels like a tunnel, dropping to the sea at the bottom. Steep, wet underfoot, and about 90 minutes if you do not stop.

places.name: Waipiʻo Valley Lookout
places.note: The rim above the valley of the kings, and as far as you get: the access road has been closed to visitors since February 2022 and pedestrians are barred too, so the only legal way down is a permitted shuttle.

places.name: Moon and Turtle
places.note: A ten-table room on Kamehameha Avenue cooking whatever the boats landed, and the best dinner on this side of the island. Reserve, and note it keeps a short week.

places.name: Two Ladies Kitchen
places.note: Mochi made by hand in a shopfront the size of a hallway, and the strawberry one is the reason for the queue. Short hours, cash, and it sells out most days, so telephone ahead.

places.name: Suisan Fish Market
places.note: The old auction house by the bay, now a poke counter where Hilo buys lunch. Eat it on the wall at Liliʻuokalani Gardens across the road.

outings.name: The Kalalau Trail to Hanakāpīʻai Falls

outings.fallback: Waimea Canyon Lookout and Puʻu Hinahina from the car park, twenty minutes each, which is most of the view for none of the effort.

outings.name: Kalalau Lookout and the Pihea ridge
outings.season: Year round. The Alakaʻi boardwalk is slick and the mud beyon

outings.name: The Awaʻawapuhi Trail
outings.season: Year round, but the clay is unusable when wet and the trail
outings.fallback: Nuʻalolo Cliff viewpoint or, if the weather has really shut in, the Kōkeʻe Natural History Museum and a bowl of chilli at the lodge.

outings.fallback: Just the Makawehi Bluff above Shipwreck Beach, forty minutes, same rock and same view of the whales in winter.

outings.name: The Līhuʻe to Kona hop
outings.season: Year round. There are only a handful of nonstops a day, so a
outings.fallback: Fly Līhuʻe to Honolulu to Kona and write off the whole day rather than the half.

outings.season: Year round. South swell in summer occasionally closes the en
outings.fallback: Kahaluʻu Beach Park in Keauhou, which has turtles, a lifeguard and a car park, and is forgiving when Hōnaunau is not.

outings.why: Boats leave Keauhou Bay at dusk, run ten minutes to a lit spot on the reef, and you hang off a float board while manta rays barrel-roll up through the plankton under you. Around $120 to $150. It is cold after forty minutes, it is crowded wi
outings.name: The manta ray night snorkel off Keauhou
outings.season: Year round. Sightings are not guaranteed and most operators
outings.fallback: The Sheraton Kona manta viewing terrace above Keauhou Bay, free, dry, and a fraction of the experience.

outings.why: Down 120 metres of rainforest switchbacks, then a mile and a half straight across the floor of a crater that was a lava lake in 1959 and still steams through the cracks. About 5.3km. The park is $30 a vehicle for seven days. Start by eight
outings.name: Kīlauea Iki crater floor loop
outings.season: Year round. The park closes sections without warning when an
outings.fallback: The Devastation Trail to Puʻu Puaʻi, 1.6km paved and flat, when the crater floor is closed for gas or the rain is horizontal.

outings.season: Entirely dependent on the eruption. Episodes have run hours
outings.fallback: Haʻakulamanu and the steam vents at dusk, then the Volcano Art Center's after-dark walk, which does not need lava to be worth the evening.

outings.season: Year round. Wind and rain at the coastal end are worse than
outings.fallback: Turn round at the Kēalakomo overlook halfway down, which is the view without the extra ninety minutes.

outings.season: Year round. Winter snow and ice close the summit road severa

outings.name: The Hāmākua run: ʻAkaka Falls, Onomea and the Waipiʻo lookout
outings.season: Year round. This is the wet side and it rains on about 270 d

destination.name: Kauaʻi and Hawaiʻi Island
destination.pitch: Two islands with almost nothing in common: Kauaʻi is one road, one canyon and a coast you can only reach on foot or by boat, and Hawaiʻi Island is a live volcano, a 4,200 metre mountain and 400km of driving, which is why ten days is the flo
destination.caveat: The middle of this trip is an airport: you return a car at Līhuʻe, fly, and collect another at Kona, and that costs most of a day, while on Kauaʻi the Hāʻena reservations that gate Kēʻe Beach and the Kalalau Trail open 30 days ahead at midnight Hawaiʻi time and sell out in minutes. Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: There is no city here. Hilo is the closest thing and it is eight blocks of old shopfronts that close at five.
because.food: Poke counters, fish markets and Sunshine Markets are the real strength. The sit-down restaurants are expensive for what they are, and outside Hanalei, Kōloa, Kona and Hilo there is very little.
because.nature: A 900 metre canyon, a rainforest that takes 9,000mm of rain a year, a coast no road reaches, and an eruption you can sometimes watch from a car park, all inside one ticket.
because.culture: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau, Limahuli Garden, the Puʻuloa petroglyphs and ʻImiloa are Hawaiian places explained by Hawaiians, not resort theatre.
because.adventure: Hanakāpīʻai Falls, the Awaʻawapuhi rim, a night swim over manta rays and a 4,200 metre summit road are all available inside one week.
because.relaxation: ʻAnini, Salt Pond and Kahaluʻu are calm water you can float in for an afternoon, and Volcano Village at 1,200 metres is cold, quiet and dark by eight.
because.exploration: Six bases, two islands, five climate zones and roads that dead-end at the thing you came for, so the driving is the trip rather than a tax on it.
